blocks.text: **Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS)** means narrowing of the space for the nerves in the lumbar spine. The narrowing can be in the central canal, the lateral recess or the exit foramen. It is usually caused by age-related changes: disc bulging, facet joint enlargement and thickening of the ligamentum flavum [Ref - to verify]. When symptoms come from the nerves, the typical picture is called **neurogenic claudication**: leg symptoms that start with walking or standing and ease with sitting or leaning forward.
A narrow canal on a scan does not always cause symptoms [Ref - to verify]. The diagnosis depends on the history and examination together with imaging.

items: Usually over 50 to 60 years old [Ref - to verify].
Pain, heaviness, numbness or weakness in the buttocks and legs, often both sides, brought on by walking or standing.
Relief by sitting, squatting or leaning forward (for example on a shopping trolley).
Back pain may be mild or present.
Symptoms are often less bothersome when cycling or when walking uphill because the spine is more flexed.

items: Observe posture (often a flexed, stooped stance) and gait. Note wide-based gait.
Spinal movement, particularly extension and the symptom response.
Neurological exam: myotomes, dermatomes, reflexes. Findings may be normal at rest, and may appear only after walking.
Peripheral pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial) and skin check.
Hip examination to exclude hip osteoarthritis.
Balance (Romberg), and upper motor neuron signs if there is gait imbalance, to exclude cervical myelopathy.
Walking test (Section E).

Standing, then walking on a flat path or treadmill at the patient's own pace

Ask the patient to walk until symptoms begin, then record time or distance. Ask them to sit and then stand and walk again; record recovery time and the posture that eases symptoms. Repeat neurological checks after walking if a deficit is suspected
Symptoms reproduced by walking and relieved by sitting or flexion
Not specific alone. Vascular claudication also appears with walking. Compare relief pattern
Check pulses and consider vascular referral if the relief pattern does not fit
Ask the patient to stand in lumbar extension for a short time (some versions use about 30 seconds) [Ref - to verify]
Leg symptoms start or increase and ease when flexing

blocks.text: Several findings support the diagnosis when combined: older age, pain below the buttock, relief on sitting, worse on walking, wide-based gait, and abnormal Romberg [Ref - to verify exact criteria]. The more of these are present, the higher the likelihood of stenosis. No single clinical sign is enough.
Pulses, capillary refill, skin colour and temperature. Weak pulses or colour change support vascular claudication. Refer for vascular assessment if suspected.

rows: Calf pain with walking, eased by standing still, weak pulses, cold skin
Usually one leg, back-and-leg pain linked to bending or sitting
Constant burning feet, not linked to walking or posture
Hand clumsiness, brisk reflexes, positive Hoffmann

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Cold, painful, pale or pulseless leg

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency flag? **Yes:** emergency.
Leg symptoms on walking and standing, eased by sitting or flexion, with preserved pulses? **Yes:** working diagnosis is neurogenic claudication from lumbar stenosis.
Weak pulses or relief only by standing still? Consider vascular referral.
Stable, mild to moderate? **Yes:** start conservative care.

Disabling walking limit, severe or progressive weakness, or no improvement after a reasonable period of conservative care? Discuss with a spine specialist about imaging and surgical opinion [Ref - to verify].

rows: Stiff painful spine, relief with flexion
Side-lying or supine knee-to-chest mobilization, gentle oscillations
Reduces compensatory stress on the lumbar spine

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** exercise and walking strategies. A combined manual therapy and exercise program has shown benefit in some trials, but evidence is limited and uncertain [Ref - to verify]. Avoid techniques that force extension. Do not claim that manual therapy widens the canal.
**Is it working?** Look for longer walking distance, easier standing and better confidence.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Build endurance in a flexed position
Easy resistance, upright or slightly forward
Walking with a support (trolley, walking poles)
Walk to first symptoms, rest in flexion, repeat several times
Lying on back, bring knees to chest

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** brief leg symptoms that settle with a short rest are acceptable. Persistent worsening, new weakness or any saddle or bladder symptoms means stop and reassess.

rows: Evidence is limited and mixed [Ref - to verify]

items: **Visit 1:** screen for CES and vascular causes; explain that symptoms are often manageable and that the aim is to improve walking and confidence.
**Early:** teach positions of relief, begin cycling or supported walking, gentle exercise.
**Middle:** build leg and trunk strength and balance; add longer walking intervals.
**Late:** return to preferred activities, self-management plan for flare-ups.
**If limited progress:** discuss specialist opinion, medication options, injection or decompression surgery with the medical team. Timing is individual and not fixed here [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: Track walking distance or time to first symptom, walking tolerance after rests, pain scale, a disability measure such as the Oswestry Disability Index or the Swiss Spinal Stenosis Questionnaire [Ref - to verify], balance, strength and falls.

rows: No change after about 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise
Review diagnosis and consider medical opinion
New weakness, falls, saddle or bladder change

blocks.text: **Case:** A 68-year-old retired teacher has bilateral buttock and thigh heaviness after 5 minutes of walking. Sitting relieves it within a minute. She can cycle for 20 minutes without symptoms. Pulses are normal, reflexes are normal at rest, no saddle or bladder symptoms.

**Working diagnosis:** lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. **Plan:** education, stationary cycling, supported walking, hip and trunk strengthening, balance, monitoring; discuss specialist referral if walking does not improve.

items: Why does leaning forward help? Flexion is thought to enlarge the space for the nerves, whereas extension may narrow it. This explanation is accepted but not fully proven for every patient.

How do you separate vascular from neurogenic claudication? Check pulses and skin, and ask what relieves symptoms. Relief by standing still suggests vascular, while relief by sitting or flexing suggests neurogenic [Ref - to verify].
Why is a scan not enough for diagnosis? Many people with a narrow canal on a scan have no symptoms, so the clinical picture matters.
When do you refer urgently? With saddle or bladder symptoms, rapidly worsening weakness or falls, or signs of acute limb ischaemia.
Why is cycling useful in this patient? The flexed position is usually better tolerated, so it allows exercise that builds fitness without provoking symptoms.
**Initial approach:** education, flexion-tolerant exercise, supported walking.
**Justifying findings:** walking-related bilateral symptoms eased by sitting or flexion, normal pulses.
**Priority:** walking tolerance, fitness and function.
**Manual therapy:** optional gentle adjunct.
**Exercise:** cycling, supported walking, leg and trunk strengthening, balance.
**Modalities:** optional comfort only.
**Tell the patient:** symptoms often improve with activity strategies; report saddle or bladder change at once.
**Avoid:** forced extension, complete rest, ignoring vascular signs.
**Measure:** time to symptoms, walking distance, ODI or SSSQ, falls.
**If no improvement:** specialist opinion.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** improved walking and confidence, self-management plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** older adult, stable symptoms, no red flags.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise programs improve walking distance and function; how surgery compares to non-surgical care.
**Hypotheses:** that flexion-based exercise works by changing canal dimensions; that cycling benefits come from posture and fitness.
**Future questions:** best exercise dose, and which patients should choose early surgery.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

items: Describe neurogenic claudication and tell it apart from vascular claudication.
Run a walking tolerance test and interpret it.

State when to refer urgently.
